Proponents of anti-miscegenation laws sometimes claimed that such laws protected women of the "superior" race from manipulation, exploitation, and degradation at the hands of men of "inferior" races. This paternalistic argument positioned white women as needing protection from predatory men of color while simultaneously positioning women of color as unworthy of similar protection.

Proponents of anti-miscegenation laws often invoked principles of federalism and states' rights, arguing that marriage regulation was properly a state matter and that federal courts should not impose national standards on state marriage laws.
